title: The Dipole Bench
summary: Build dipoles, hold them against a field, test their stability and measure how their field fades with distance.
subject: physics
concepts: Torque on a dipole in a uniform field
Field on the axis and the equatorial plane
learningOutcome: The student can find a dipole moment, the torque on a dipole in a field, which orientation is stable, the axis and equatorial fields, and how the field falls with distance.

levels.title: Build a dipole
levels.adds: Baseline: the dipole moment is p = q × 2a, pointing from − to +, and a dipole has zero total charge (Ex 1.9).
hints: p = q × 2a. Convert nC to coulombs and cm to metres.
The moment points from the negative charge to the positive charge.
The two charges are equal and opposite, so the total charge is zero.

levels.title: Hold it still
levels.adds: New idea: a uniform field gives a dipole no net force but a torque τ = pE sin θ (Ex 1.10).
hints: The field pulls +q and −q with equal and opposite forces qE, so the net force is zero.
The torque is τ = p E sin θ, where θ is the angle between p and E.
The torque turns the dipole towards the field.

levels.title: Which way is stable?
levels.adds: New idea: a dipole is in stable equilibrium along the field and in unstable equilibrium against it.
hints: The torque is zero when p is along the field or against it.
Nudge it: if the torque turns it back, the equilibrium is stable.
Along the field a nudge is corrected; against it a nudge grows until the dipole flips round.

levels.title: Axis or equator?
levels.adds: New idea: far away the field is 2kp/r³ along p on the axis and kp/r³ against p on the equator (Example 1.9).
hints: On the axis (the line through both charges) E = 2kp/r³, along the moment.
On the equatorial plane E = kp/r³, pointing against the moment.
Use r in metres and p = q × 2a in C m.

levels.title: How fast it fades
levels.adds: New idea: a dipole’s field falls as 1/r³, faster than the 1/r² of a single charge.
hints: Far away E ∝ 1/r³, so doubling the distance divides the field by 8.
To fall to a fraction f the distance must grow by k = (1/f)^(1/3).
A single charge needs k = (1/f)^(1/2): the dipole fades faster.

misconceptions: A dipole has no field because its total charge is zero
A dipole in a uniform field is pulled sideways
A dipole is stable in any orientation
The field of a dipole falls as 1/r²
